speakerBio: Nephrologist with a joint liver-unit practice who teaches that the kidney measures the arterial tree, not the tank, and that most 'hepatorenal syndrome' on the take is really over-diuresis until proven otherwise.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 58-year-old man with known alcoholic cirrhosis is admitted with a tense ascites and worsening confusion. His blood pressure is 96/58, he is deeply jaundiced, and his creatinine has climbed from a baseline of 70 to 185 µmol/L over ten days. The night registrar, spotting the low blood pressure and dry-looking tongue, has already run in two litres of saline "for the pre-renal picture" — and nothing has happened; the creatinine is still climbing and now the ascites is worse. Here is the diagnostic knot this session unties: this man's kidney is being throttled by vasoconstriction and it is sensing an empty arterial tree — yet he is not fluid-deplete at all. He has a full tank pooled in the wrong compartment. The distinction between true hypovolaemia and reduced effective circulating volume is the difference between a bag of fluid curing your patient and a bag of fluid drowning him. And at the far end of that spectrum sits hepatorenal syndrome.

1 · 💧 Pre-renal AKI — the volume-responsive kidney

Pre-renal AKI is, by definition, a functional and reversible state: the parenchyma is structurally normal and the entire problem is that renal perfusion has fallen below what autoregulation can defend. The kidney responds exactly as designed — it activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis and vasopressin, clamps down to retain salt and water, and concentrates the urine. Every classic pre-renal finding is simply the fingerprint of a healthy tubule fighting to hold on to sodium and water:

  • Low urine sodium (<20 mmol/L) — aldosterone-driven avid sodium reabsorption.
  • Concentrated urine (osmolality >500 mOsm/kg) — vasopressin-driven water retention.
  • Raised urea:creatinine ratio — urea is passively reabsorbed with the avidly-reabsorbed water, rising out of proportion to creatinine.
  • Bland urinary sediment — no casts of significance, because no cell is dying.
  • Prompt reversibility — restore perfusion and the creatinine falls within 24–72 hours.
Pre-renal AKI is the kidney working perfectly in a failing circulation. The cure is not for the kidney — it is for the circulation.

The causes divide cleanly into true volume loss (haemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, burns, pancreatitis) and circulatory failure with a normal or expanded volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, sepsis). The urine indices look identical in both — the kidney cannot tell why it is underperfused, only that it is — which is exactly why treatment diverges so dangerously.

2 · 🧪 Fractional excretion of sodium — reading the tubule's intent

The single most useful bedside chemistry in the pre-renal-versus-ATN question is the fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) — the percentage of filtered sodium that the kidney actually excretes rather than reclaims:

FeNa (%) = (UNa × PCr) ÷ (PNa × UCr) × 100
FeNaInterpretationMechanism
< 1%Pre-renalTubule intact and hoarding sodium — reabsorbing >99% of filtered Na⁺
> 2%Established ATNDead tubule cannot reabsorb — sodium leaks into the urine
1–2%IndeterminateEarly/evolving, or a mixed picture

A FeNa <1% says "this tubule is alive and desperately conserving sodium" — the hallmark of a pre-renal state (and, importantly, of some intrinsic causes with intact tubules, like acute glomerulonephritis, contrast nephropathy early on, and hepatorenal syndrome). A FeNa >2% says "this tubule has stopped reabsorbing" — the hallmark of ATN.

⚠️ FeNa is a trap in the diuretic-treated patient

A loop or thiazide diuretic forces sodium into the urine by blocking its reabsorption — so a genuinely pre-renal, volume-deplete patient on furosemide will have a falsely high FeNa (>2%), mimicking ATN. This is a common error in the heart-failure and cirrhotic patient, who are almost always diuretic-loaded. Other confounders: CKD (baseline sodium wasting raises FeNa), sepsis and early contrast/pigment nephropathy (paradoxically low FeNa despite tubular injury). Never read a FeNa without the drug chart in your other hand.

3 · 🔬 Fractional excretion of urea — the diuretic workaround

Because diuretics wreck the FeNa, the fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea) is the go-to alternative. Urea is reabsorbed proximally, upstream of where loop and thiazide diuretics act, so it is relatively protected from their confounding effect:

FeUrea (%) = (UUrea × PCr) ÷ (PUrea × UCr) × 100.   <35% = pre-renal; >50% = ATN.
IndexPre-renalATNMain pitfall
FeNa<1%>2%Falsely high with diuretics; low in CKD, sepsis, contrast, GN
FeUrea<35%>50%More reliable on diuretics, but less specific overall
💡 When your patient is on furosemide, switch to FeUrea

Because urea is handled proximally, before the loop and distal tubule where diuretics act, FeUrea stays interpretable when FeNa has been sabotaged by a diuretic. A FeUrea <35% still points to a volume-responsive, pre-renal kidney even in the fully diureticised heart-failure or cirrhotic patient. Neither index is perfect — they inform, not decide.

4 · 🎭 True hypovolaemia vs reduced effective circulating volume

This is the conceptual heart of the session. The kidney does not sense your total body water — it senses the effective arterial blood volume (EABV), the fraction of the circulation actually stretching the arterial baroreceptors and perfusing the afferent arteriole. Two utterly different physiological states can drop the EABV to the same low value:

FeatureTrue hypovolaemiaReduced effective circulating volume
Total body waterLow (tank is empty)Normal or high (tank is full or overflowing)
Classic causesHaemorrhage, D&V, diuresis, burnsHeart failure, cirrhosis, sepsis, nephrotic syndrome
Where the volume isGenuinely lost from the bodyMis-distributed — venous congestion, ascites, oedema, splanchnic pooling
Clinical signsDry mucosae, ↓ skin turgor, ↓ JVP, postural dropRaised JVP, oedema, ascites, S3 — wet despite an under-filled artery
Correct treatmentGive fluidTreat the circulation (offload, vasoconstrict, treat the cause) — fluid often harms

Both light up the same renal salt-and-water-retaining reflexes, so both give a low urine sodium and a low FeNa. But in true hypovolaemia the retained fluid refills the tank and cures the kidney; in reduced EABV the retained fluid pours into the third space — worsening the ascites, the oedema, the pulmonary congestion — while the arterial under-filling that the kidney is reacting to barely improves. Give a litre of saline to the decompensated cirrhotic and you have not filled his arteries; you have enlarged his ascites.

The kidney measures the arterial tree, not the tank. In heart failure and cirrhosis the tank is full but the artery is empty — pouring in more fluid fills the wrong compartment.
🎯 The two axes teased in session 1, now made concrete

Cardiorenal: the failing pump cannot generate forward flow, and rising venous pressure congests the kidney from behind — so the artery is under-filled while the veins are engorged. Hepatorenal: splanchnic arterial vasodilation steals the circulating volume into the gut bed — so the artery is under-filled while the abdomen fills with ascites. Same renal reflexes, opposite fluid strategies to the volume-deplete patient.

5 · 🫀 Hepatorenal syndrome — the vicious cycle, drawn out

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI) is the extreme end of the reduced-EABV spectrum: a functionally normal kidney shut down by a systemic vascular catastrophe of cirrhosis. The mechanism is a self-reinforcing loop worth drawing step by step:

  1. Portal hypertension drives release of nitric oxide and other vasodilators in the splanchnic circulation.
  2. Splanchnic arterial vasodilation pools blood in the gut vasculature — the effective arterial blood volume collapses even as total volume (ascites!) rises.
  3. The under-filled arterial tree triggers maximal activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system and vasopressin.
  4. These systemic vasoconstrictors clamp down hardest on the renal arterioles — intense renal vasoconstriction, collapsing GFR.
  5. The kidney retains yet more salt and water, feeding the ascites and further splanchnic pooling — the cycle tightens.

Crucially the kidney itself is structurally normal — HRS kidneys have been transplanted into recipients and worked normally. This is a haemodynamic diagnosis, and therefore a diagnosis of exclusion.

Diagnostic criteria (ICA / HRS-AKI)

  • Cirrhosis with ascites, meeting the KDIGO definition of AKI.
  • No sustained improvement after ≥2 days of diuretic withdrawal and volume expansion with albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day).
  • Absence of shock.
  • No current/recent nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast).
  • No structural kidney injury: proteinuria <500 mg/day, no microhaematuria, normal renal ultrasound.
💡 HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion — the albumin challenge does the excluding

You cannot call HRS until you have proven the kidney is not simply volume-deplete. That is what the 48-hour albumin challenge (1 g/kg/day) plus diuretic withdrawal does: if the creatinine falls, it was pre-renal from over-diuresis or hypovolaemia; if it does not, and there is no shock, nephrotoxin or structural disease, you are left with HRS. Albumin is chosen over saline because it stays in the vascular space and specifically expands the under-filled arterial volume.

6 · 💊 Treating HRS — vasoconstrictors, albumin, and the CONFIRM trial

The treatment logic follows the mechanism exactly: if the problem is splanchnic vasodilation stealing the arterial volume, then splanchnic vasoconstriction plus volume expansion should reverse it. That is precisely what works:

TherapyMechanismRole
Terlipressin + albuminVasopressin analogue → splanchnic vasoconstriction, restoring arterial volume; albumin expands it furtherFirst-line pharmacological therapy for HRS-AKI
Noradrenaline + albuminSystemic vasoconstrictionICU alternative where terlipressin unavailable
Midodrine + octreotide + albuminOral vasoconstrictor + splanchnic vasoconstrictorOlder/less effective regimen
TIPSDecompresses portal hypertensionSelected patients; can improve renal function
Liver transplantationCures the underlying diseaseDefinitive — the only durable cure

Terlipressin + albumin is the cornerstone. The CONFIRM trial (Wong et al., NEJM 2021), the largest randomised trial in HRS, showed terlipressin significantly improved the rate of HRS reversal versus placebo (verified reversal ~29% vs 16%). The punchline is nuanced: it reverses HRS but did not improve overall survival, and it came at a real cost — respiratory failure (a recognised terlipressin adverse effect, driving an FDA boxed warning) and other ischaemic events. So terlipressin buys renal recovery and a bridge, but it is not benign and it is not a cure.

Terlipressin squeezes the leaking splanchnic bed shut and albumin fills the artery — reversing HRS, but watch for respiratory failure, and remember only the liver transplant actually cures it.
🎯 HRS is a bridge-to-transplant problem

Because HRS is driven by the failing liver, medical therapy — terlipressin, albumin, TIPS — is fundamentally a bridge. Reversing the creatinine improves transplant candidacy and peri-operative outcomes, but the durable cure is liver transplantation. Every HRS patient should be discussed with a transplant centre.

☠️ M&M — the reversible kidney they called irreversible

A 61-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites was admitted with a creatinine of 210 (baseline 68). She had been discharged a week earlier on high-dose spironolactone and furosemide after a diuresis for peripheral oedema, and had since had poor oral intake. On admission a junior team, recognising 'cirrhosis + rising creatinine', labelled her hepatorenal syndrome, started terlipressin, and referred her as a poor transplant candidate. But nobody had done the two things the HRS criteria demand first: stop the diuretics and give an albumin challenge. She was, in fact, simply over-diuresed and volume-deplete — a straightforward, reversible pre-renal AKI masquerading as HRS. Her FeNa was misleadingly high (she was loaded with furosemide), which had falsely reassured the team it 'wasn't pre-renal'. When a nephrologist finally withdrew the diuretics and ran the 1 g/kg/day albumin challenge, her creatinine fell to 95 within 48 hours. Lessons: HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion — you must withdraw diuretics and volume-expand with albumin before you can invoke it; a high FeNa in a diureticised patient is uninterpretable (use FeUrea, or better, the albumin challenge itself); and mislabelling a reversible pre-renal state as HRS exposes the patient to terlipressin's risks, delays the real fix, and can wrongly downgrade a transplant candidate. Always empty the differential of the reversible before you name the irreversible.

7 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Pre-renal AKI is functional and reversible — a structurally normal kidney working perfectly in a failing circulation; the cure is for the circulation, not the kidney.
  2. FeNa <1% = pre-renal, >2% = ATN — it reads whether the tubule is still hoarding sodium — but it is falsely high on diuretics and confounded by CKD, sepsis and contrast.
  3. When the patient is diureticised, switch to FeUrea (<35% pre-renal, >50% ATN), since urea is handled proximally, upstream of diuretic action.
  4. The kidney senses effective arterial blood volume, not total body water — so heart failure and cirrhosis give a low FeNa and every pre-renal sign while the tank is full; giving fluid fills the wrong compartment.
  5. HRS-AKI is a vicious cycle: portal hypertension → splanchnic vasodilation → collapsed EABV → RAAS/vasopressin activation → intense renal vasoconstriction; the kidney is structurally normal.
  6. HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion confirmed by no response to diuretic withdrawal + albumin 1 g/kg/day for 48h, absence of shock, nephrotoxins and structural disease.
  7. Terlipressin + albumin is first-line (CONFIRM: improved HRS reversal, no survival benefit, beware respiratory failure); TIPS helps selected patients; liver transplant is the only cure.

moderatorQs.q: A patient with decompensated heart failure has a low urine sodium and a FeNa of 0.4%, yet is grossly oedematous with a raised JVP. Why, and how does it change management?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the kidney senses the effective arterial blood volume, not total body water. In heart failure the pump cannot generate forward flow and the arterial tree is under-filled, so the kidney activates RAAS, sympathetic tone and vasopressin and avidly retains sodium — giving a low urine sodium and a FeNa <1% — exactly as if the patient were haemorrhaging. But the tank is not empty; it is overflowing into the interstitium and lungs, which is why the JVP is up and the patient is oedematous. The management implication is the opposite of true hypovolaemia: giving fluid fills the wrong compartment and worsens congestion. Instead you treat the circulation — decongest (diurese, sometimes with the paradox that offloading venous congestion improves renal perfusion by lowering renal venous pressure), optimise cardiac output and afterload, and treat the underlying cardiac cause. The low FeNa here is a clue to the physiology, not a licence to give saline.

moderatorQs.q: Walk us through the pathophysiological cascade of hepatorenal syndrome, and explain why the treatment is a vasoconstrictor.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It is a self-tightening loop. Portal hypertension drives nitric-oxide-mediated splanchnic arterial vasodilation, which pools the circulating volume in the gut bed and collapses the effective arterial blood volume — even though total volume is high (ascites). The under-filled artery triggers maximal RAAS, sympathetic and vasopressin activation, and these systemic vasoconstrictors clamp down hardest on the renal arterioles, collapsing GFR; the resulting salt-and-water retention feeds the ascites and further splanchnic pooling, tightening the cycle. The kidney itself is structurally normal. Because the root problem is arterial under-filling from a leaking splanchnic bed, the logical treatment is a splanchnic vasoconstrictor — terlipressin — plus albumin to expand the arterial volume: you squeeze the dilated splanchnic vessels shut, restore effective arterial volume, switch off the renal vasoconstrictor drive, and GFR recovers.

moderatorQs.q: What did the CONFIRM trial show about terlipressin in HRS, and how does that shape your expectations of the drug?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: CONFIRM (Wong et al., NEJM 2021) was the largest randomised placebo-controlled trial of terlipressin (with albumin) in HRS-AKI. It showed terlipressin significantly improved the rate of HRS reversal / verified reversal (roughly 29% vs 16% with placebo). The crucial caveats that shape expectations: it did not improve overall survival, and it carried meaningful harm — notably respiratory failure (contributing to an FDA boxed warning) and ischaemic adverse events. So I expect terlipressin to reverse the renal failure in a minority and buy a bridge, improving transplant candidacy and peri-operative physiology, rather than to cure the patient or prolong life on its own. It reinforces that HRS is fundamentally a bridge-to-liver-transplant problem, and that terlipressin must be used with careful monitoring for fluid overload and respiratory compromise.

audienceQs.q: My cirrhotic patient is on furosemide and spironolactone. Their FeNa is 3% — does that rule out a pre-renal cause?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — in a diureticised patient a high FeNa is essentially uninterpretable. Loop and thiazide diuretics force sodium into the urine by blocking its reabsorption, so a genuinely volume-deplete, pre-renal patient will show a falsely elevated FeNa that mimics ATN. Do two things: switch to the fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea), which is handled proximally, upstream of the diuretics, and stays interpretable (<35% still suggests pre-renal); and, because this is a cirrhotic, actually run the diagnostic manoeuvre that matters — withdraw the diuretics and give an albumin challenge (1 g/kg/day for 48h). If the creatinine falls, it was pre-renal from over-diuresis; if it does not, you are moving toward hepatorenal syndrome. Don't let a diuretic-corrupted FeNa talk you out of a reversible diagnosis.

audienceQs.q: Why do we give albumin rather than normal saline to expand volume in a cirrhotic with AKI?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because the problem is under-filling of the arterial compartment, and albumin is far better at expanding it. Albumin is a large oncotic molecule that stays in the vascular space, so it pulls and holds volume in the circulation and specifically raises the effective arterial blood volume that the kidney is reacting to. Crystalloid like saline distributes across the whole extracellular space and, in a cirrhotic with low oncotic pressure and portal hypertension, largely leaks straight into the ascites and interstitium — expanding the third space without meaningfully filling the artery. Albumin (1 g/kg/day, max 100 g/day) is also the agreed volume challenge in the HRS diagnostic criteria and is used with terlipressin and after large-volume paracentesis for the same physiological reason.

audienceQs.q: When would you reach for noradrenaline instead of terlipressin in HRS, and what's the endpoint?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Noradrenaline plus albumin is the practical ICU alternative when terlipressin is unavailable, contraindicated, or when the patient is already in a critical-care setting needing an arterial line and close haemodynamic monitoring. Both work by the same logic — systemic/splanchnic vasoconstriction to restore effective arterial volume and switch off the renal vasoconstrictor drive. The endpoint is reversal of HRS: a fall in creatinine toward baseline, usually targeted via a rise in mean arterial pressure (aiming for an increase of around 10–15 mmHg, e.g. a MAP goal of ~85 mmHg) and a recovering urine output, given alongside daily albumin. Throughout, watch for the ischaemic and fluid-overload complications of vasoconstriction, and keep the patient anchored to the real endpoint — bridging to liver transplantation, the only durable cure.
